title: The basket in the reeds (Exodus 2:1–10)
hook: a mother, a sister watching, a princess who pities a crying baby

segments.voice: Yesterday, the midwives: Shiphrah and Puah feared God more than Pharaoh. Your line was two women said no.

When the midwives won't do it, Pharaoh stops pretending. He orders all his people: every son born to the Hebrews, throw him into the river. Into this, a baby boy is born to a family from the tribe of Levi. His mother sees, the text says, that he is a goodly child, and she hides him for three months. Three months of a newborn, hidden: the crying, the night feedings, the neighbors. Then he gets too big and too loud to hide.
screen: `THROW THEM IN THE RIVER.` → `A GOODLY CHILD.` → `HIDDEN THREE MONTHS.`

segments.voice: So she does something brave and strange. In the King James Bible: "she took for him an ark of bulrushes, and daubed it with slime and with pitch, and put the child therein; and she laid it in the flags by the river's brink." An ark. The Hebrew word is tevah, the same word Genesis uses for Noah's ark: once a boat that carried the whole world through the flood, now a little one, sealed with tar, carrying one baby. She puts him in the very river Pharaoh wanted him thrown into. "And his sister stood afar off, to wit what would be done to him." Someone was watching. Then Pharaoh's daughter comes down to bathe. She has the basket brought and opens it, "and, behold, the babe wept. And she had compassion on him." She knows he's one of the Hebrews' children, and she keeps him anyway, against her own father's order. Now the sister moves: shall I find a Hebrew woman to nurse him for you? Go, says the princess. So the sister brings back the baby's own mother, who is paid to nurse her own son. When he's older, the princess adopts him and names him: "Because I drew him out of the water." Moses. Look at who saves him: a mother, a sister, a foreign princess, and before them, two midwives. Not one of them is a king or a soldier, and the one with royal blood is defying her own father. Every one of them was paying attention. Some Christian readers notice another baby, in Matthew's Gospel, whose life was threatened by a king, carried to safety in Egypt.
screen: `AN ARK OF BULRUSHES.` · `TEVAH: NOAH'S WORD.` · `HIS SISTER STOOD AFAR OFF.` · `THE BABE WEPT. SHE HAD COMPASSION.` · then, large: `BECAUSE I DREW HIM OUT OF THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Think of someone small in your life: a child, a grandchild, a neighbor's kid, or someone small in another way, a person easily overlooked. Picture yourself like the sister, standing a little way off, watching to see what will happen to them, ready to step in. If you pray, you can pray for them by name; if not, simply hold them in mind.
Tevah. Hebrew for ark, the same word for Noah's: the little basket of bulrushes where a mother hid her baby in the Nile.
Your line: someone was watching. Sometimes from a little way off, and that's enough. Day three hundred seventy-nine, done.

howItsDone: Christians tell the story of baby Moses to children, and some read it alongside Matthew 2, where the infant Jesus escapes King Herod; churches use it to speak about protecting children and welcoming adopted and foster children.

chat.says: Why was baby Moses put in a basket on the river?
options: His mother hid him from Pharaoh's order, sealed him in a little ark, and his sister watched.
Pharaoh's daughter had asked for a Hebrew baby, so his mother sent him to her.
His family was too poor to feed him, so they hoped a rich stranger would.
chat.meaning: Pharaoh ordered Hebrew baby boys thrown into the river. His mother hid him, then set him in a tevah, and his sister watched.

tevah.meaning: Hebrew for ark, used for Noah's boat and this basket

Levi.meaning: one of Israel's tribes; Moses's family came from it

bulrushes.meaning: tall reeds that grow by the river

Matthew's Gospel.meaning: one of the four Gospels, telling the life of Jesus

notes: tevah used only for Noah's ark (Genesis 6–9) and Moses's basket (Exodus 2:3, 5): standard; confirm.
The sister is unnamed here; tradition identifies her as Miriam (named later). The script leaves her unnamed.
Moses: Hebrew folk etymology from mashah ('draw out'); Egyptian msi/ms ('born/son') as in Thutmose. Confirm.
Matthew 2 parallel (a king threatening infants; flight to Egypt) presented as something Christians have long noticed.
